headline: New moon springs load up The Race and Plum Gut as fluke abandon the baking bay
subhead: Stripers stack the eddies on max current, bluefish chop through Orient, and the fluke bite has gone from Peconic mud to cold ocean water pouring through the inlets.
body_markdown:
Last week the Sound did what it always does heading into a new moon — the current built every tide, and by Sunday The Race was running like a river. Wind had been out of the northeast for a stretch, which kept some chop stacked against Fishers Island but also pushed a slug of cooler water up against the eastern grounds. That mattered, because Gardiners Bay and the Peconics have been sitting up near 78 degrees, borderline uncomfortable for fluke, while the ocean-side water pushing through Plum Gut and Orient on the incoming has been running closer to 71. That 7-degree gap is the whole story of the week — everything that can leave the warm shallow water for the cold moving water has been doing exactly that.

This week the moon goes new on the 11th, which means we're building toward spring tides right through the weekend — bigger swings, harder current, and a PM flood that starts stacking up against sunset from Friday through Monday. That's the window I'm circling. When the evening high tide lines up with last light at Plum Gut and Orient Point, the bass come up out of the depth and feed the last hour of shrinking light into full dark. It's not a guarantee, but I've fished that convergence enough summers to know it's the best two hours you'll get all week if the wind cooperates.

Striper fishing right now is a current game, full stop. The bite at The Race and Plum Gut is happening on the meat of the tide, not the slack — find the eddy behind Valiant Rock or off North Dumnpling where five knots of water folds back on itself, and that's where the bass are parked, facing into the current waiting for whatever gets swept past. Eels fished on a fish-finder rig, weighted just enough to hold bottom in that current, have been the most consistent producer after dark. Guys throwing big Danny-style swimmers and bucktail-and-eelskin combos off the rocks at Orient Point State Park have connected too, mostly on the last two hours of the incoming into the top of the tide. Sizes have been mixed — plenty of schoolies and mid-20s in the mix, but there are still pockets of genuinely large fish showing up in that current, the kind that make your drag sing when a 40-incher decides it doesn't want to come off bottom. Nothing guaranteed, but the fish are there — you need to be on the water when the current's running hardest, which usually means 10 p.m. to 2 a.m. right now.

Bluefish have been the more reliable player. Choppers in the 8-to-12-pound class are working bunker schools through Plum Gut and off Orient Point on the ebb, and they're not subtle about it — surface blitzes with birds working overhead, easy to spot from the boat or even from the rocks at first light. Bunker spoons trolled behind the boat at 3-4 knots have been money, and if you want to cast, a Hogy popper or a chrome Kastmaster worked fast through the froth will get bit. This bite has been the most dependable thing in the zone the past ten days — less finesse than the bass game, more about being in the right piece of moving water when the bait gets pushed through the funnel.

Fluke is where the story's changed the most. The bay bite has gone soft as that Peconic water climbed into the high 70s — fish just don't want to work that hard in warm water when there's cooler stuff nearby. What's happened instead is a real push of fluke out of the bay and into the current-swept edges: Orient Harbor's outer channel, the deeper cuts inside Plum Gut, and the drop-offs on the ocean side of Fishers Island. Fishing the last two hours of the outgoing in 25 to 40 feet with a 3/4-ounce white bucktail and a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet has been the play — drift slow, keep contact with bottom, and expect the bite to come as a subtle tick rather than a slam. Sizes have been decent, some fish pushing 4 to 5 pounds mixed in with a lot of shorts, so it's not a keeper-every-drift situation, but the fish are there if you put the time in on the right piece of structure.

Porgies have been quiet and dependable at the same time — not exciting, but a sure thing if you want dinner. The rock piles off Fishers Island and around Bug Light are holding good numbers in 20 to 30 feet, and a simple high-low rig with sandworms or clam strips will keep you busy on any stage of the tide. Weakfish, on the other hand, I'm not seeing. Water temps have been right for weeks now and there's still nothing worth reporting — I'd put my money elsewhere.

One more thing worth watching: the warm-water pelagic window that's been building along the South Shore inlets is in its final days, and there's a real chance the first bonito or Spanish mackerel push into the strong current at Plum Gut or The Race before it closes out. I haven't seen it yet in our water, but the current here is exactly the kind of structure those fish like to work, and the timing lines up. If I had a morning open this week, I'd be running light spinning gear with small metal jigs just in case, while still working the main program — bass on the current, blues on the blitz, fluke on the drift. That's the reliable stuff. The bonito would just be a bonus.
